verses.translation_literal: In you, YHWH, I have taken refuge; may I not be ashamed to the age.
verses.translation_dramatic: In you, O LORD, I have taken shelter. Let me never, never be put to shame.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm has no heading, no 'a psalm of David', no 'to the choirmaster', and opens in mid-breath, as if it were the continuation of Psalm 70's cry for help (Radak and Meiri both say it was recited right after it). Play it as a man already at the door of the shelter. The first word is 'in you', put before the divine name: the whole prayer is placed on this one address.

KJV 'put to confusion' and 'put my trust' are both a little slack. The verb ḥāsâ is physical: to run under cover, as a bird under wings or a fugitive into a rock cleft. And bôsh is not mere embarrassment but public disgrace, being shown to have bet on the wrong power. In the honour-and-shame world of the ancient Near East, to lose the bet is to lose standing before all. 'For ever' (lĕ'ôlām) can be heard as 'to the age', a long horizon, so the plea is for a lasting verdict, not a rescue for tonight. Lines 1-3 nearly repeat Psalm 31:2-4, which shows how liturgical language was shared and reused.

philological_notes.note: To take refuge: the image is bodily shelter from danger, not an inner feeling of trust. The perfect describes an act already done and, as Meiri sees, may carry a present or future force ('in you I take refuge').
'Let me be ashamed' (cohortative after 'al, a wish). Shame here is public humiliation when the one trusted fails to act.

verses.translation_literal: In your righteousness you will rescue me and you will deliver me; incline to me your ear and save me.
verses.translation_dramatic: By your own justice, rescue me. Bring me out. Bend down your ear to me, and save me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four pleas in one breath: rescue, deliver, incline, save. Let them crowd each other; there is no pause between them in the Hebrew. The speaker does not appeal to his own merit but to God's tsedaqah, here the faithfulness of a king and judge to put right what is wrong (Metzudat David: 'not by the reward of deeds'; Radak even has David knowing he is paying for his own sin).

KJV 'Deliver me in thy righteousness' turns the two imperfects into commands and lets 'righteousness' sound like a moral quality. The Hebrew verbs are in the form 'you will rescue me': half statement of confidence, half plea. 'Incline your ear' is a physical picture: a great one leaning down from his throne to catch the voice of a small person. BBE's 'give ear to my voice' adds a word the Hebrew lacks.

philological_notes.note: God's righteousness in the sense of acting rightly as judge and saviour, putting right the oppressed; not an abstract moral perfection.

verses.translation_literal: Be to me for a rock of dwelling, to go in continually; you have commanded to save me, for my crag and my stronghold are you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be my rock, my home, the place I may always come to. You have already given the word that I be saved, for you are my crag, my stronghold, you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is a cave-fortress in the Judean hills, a cleft in the rock where a fugitive can go in and be out of reach. Hold 'to go in continually' as the point: not one emergency, but a door that is always open. The word order saves the pronoun 'you' for the very last word, a spotlight on the one addressed.

KJV 'strong habitation' is a fair guess, but ma'ôn is a dwelling or lair, and in the rest of the verse the picture is rock and fortress, so the 'habitation' is carved into stone. 'Thou hast given commandment' is correct but the jussive reading matters: the sense is that God has already issued the order. Tradition says God commands angels (Rashi, Radak and Meiri cite Ps 91:11), so rescue is carried out by messengers. The verse closely parallels Psalm 31:3-4, where the Hebrew reads ma'ôz 'refuge' for ma'ôn.

philological_notes.note: A dwelling or refuge, sometimes an animal's lair; the parallel in Psalm 31:3 reads מָעוֹז 'stronghold'.
'You have commanded': for Rashi and Radak the command is given to God's messengers (angels), and the perfect may stand for 'you will command'.
A mountain stronghold or fastness; from the root 'to hunt', the same word also means a net or hunting-place, here a place where the hunted is out of reach.

verses.translation_literal: My God, rescue me from [the] hand of [the] wicked, from [the] palm of [one who acts] perversely and [one who is] ruthless.
verses.translation_dramatic: My God. Pull me out. Out of the hand of the wicked one, out of the grip of the man who bends what is right, the man who tears and takes.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a cry from a man already held. The speaker names two grips: the yad, the open hand that reaches, and the kaf, the palm that closes round what it has caught. The second word is the tighter one, and Malbim hears exactly that in the change: the palm is more than the hand, as if the enemy has already seized him. 'Rescue' (palet) is the verb of an escape from a trap, a slipping out, not a courtroom acquittal. In a world without police, a poor or old man had no court to turn to against a strong man, so the only appeal was to God as the judge who sits above the village elders.

The KJV, 'the unrighteous and cruel man', is faithful to the three terms in the Hebrew (wicked, unrighteous, cruel) and adds only the noun 'man', so that the two participles me'avvel and chometz, who in Hebrew are bare descriptions, become adjectives of one man. The Hebrew keeps them as two ways of being: one who warps justice, and one who is ruthless. The KJV also says 'out of the hand' twice, where the Hebrew uses two different words, yad and kaf, and the variation is lost. Chometz is rare. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion tie it to the 'oppressed' or 'violent' of Isaiah 1:17 and to chamas, 'violence'; the same root gives the word for leaven and vinegar, so a sour, biting cruelty may sound under it. Radak names Absalom and Ahithophel here, a reading that belongs to his tradition of reading the psalm as David's.

philological_notes.note: 'From the palm of'. Kaf is the hollow of the hand, the closed grasp, where yad is the hand generally. Malbim reads the shift from yad to kaf as an intensification: the enemy has already taken hold.

A rare participle, 'ruthless' or 'oppressor'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion link it to the 'oppressed' of Isaiah 1:17 (chamots) and to chamas, 'violence'. The root's ordinary sense, 'be sour, leavened', may colour it.

verses.translation_literal: For you are my hope, Lord YHWH, my confidence from my youth.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you are my hope, Lord, LORD, my one sure ground since the days I was young.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'for' gives the reason for everything asked so far. A beat of memory: the voice drops and the speaker looks back down the years. 'From my youth' is the first of the psalm's two time-depths, youth now and the womb in the next verse; Radak hears it as early recognition of God, Malbim as the past tense of trust, set against 'hope' for the future.

KJV 'O Lord God' is the usual avoidance of 'Lord YHWH' (the second word is the divine name written with the vowels of Elohim, to keep readers from saying it). 'Hope' (tiqwâ) is not wishing: its root is the cord or line, and it means what you hold on to while waiting. 'Trust' for mibṭaḥ is a place or object of confidence, a refuge, rather than the act.

philological_notes.note: Hope, from the verb 'to wait expectantly', related to a taut cord; the thing hope hangs on.
From my youth; plural of the abstract noun, 'the time of youth'. Meiri hears an allusion to the beginning of the exile, Radak to David's early knowledge of God.

verses.translation_literal: On you I have leaned from the belly, from the inward parts of my mother; you are the one who cut me off [brought me out]; in you is my praise continually.
verses.translation_dramatic: On you I have leaned since before I drew breath, since I lay in my mother's body. You are the one who drew me out into the light. In you my praise has its home, always.
verses.directors_commentary:
From youth the psalm goes back further, to the womb, and the speaker places the first act of dependence before birth. The midwife here is God. The word for 'womb' is not the polite one: me'ê 'immî are the inward parts, the 'guts' or bowels of the mother. KJV and ASV keep 'bowels' and are right to; BBE's 'body' and Webster's 'brought me into life' sand it down.

The verb gôzî is the hard word. By the pointing it is from gāzâ 'cut off, sever', so 'you are the one who cut me off' (as the cord), YLT renders it so. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion tie it to wayyāgāz in Numbers 11:31, quails 'brought' from the sea. A modern emendation to gōḥî (Ps 22:10 'who drew me out') is possible; either way the picture is God as midwife. 'Leaned' (nismakti) is bodily: a person resting weight on a wall or staff.

philological_notes.note: Rare. Taken as 'cut off' (the cord), or 'brought out', as in Numbers 11:31; Meiri compares gôḥî, 'the one who draws me out' (Ps 22:10).
'From my mother's inward parts', the frank anatomical word that the speaker uses for birth; it names the organs, not an abstract 'womb'.
Reflexive: 'I have propped myself, leaned my weight'.

token_glosses.gloss: the one who brought me out (cut me off)

verses.translation_literal: Like a portent I have become to many; and you are my refuge of strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: To many I have become a sign, a thing to stare at and whisper about. But you are my refuge, my strong place.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has become an object lesson. A mofet is a portent or sign, something striking that others point to as a warning; Ezekiel is called one in Ezekiel 24:24, which Rashi and Ibn Ezra both cite. Play the line with a downward look: people see him and say 'that could be us' (Rashi).

KJV 'a wonder unto many' leans on the older meaning of 'wonder' as a marvel, and misses the dark half: the same word is a sign of judgment. The sentence turns on 'and you' (wĕ'attâ), a strong contrast. 'Refuge of strength' (maḥsî-'ōz) is a construct chain; KJV 'strong refuge' and BBE 'strong tower' fine, though Meiri notes that 'refuge' is short for 'a refuge of strength'. Malbim reads mofet as an object of wonder, because his success looked beyond nature, not as a warning, and that is a legitimate alternative.

philological_notes.note: A sign or portent; may be a marvel or an exemplary warning. In Ezekiel 24:24 the prophet is a mofet to the people.

verses.translation_literal: My mouth is filled [with] your praise, all the day [with] your splendor.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my mouth be full of your praise, full of your splendor, all the day long.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone lifts after the dark of verse 7. The mouth that once only begged is now to be filled, as a vessel is filled. The verb is imperfect and can be read as a wish ('let it be filled') or a vow ('it will be filled'); Radak makes it a promise that follows rescue, Ibn Ezra the answer to 'in you is my praise' in verse 6.

KJV 'honour' for tif'ārâ weakens it: the word is splendor, beauty, what makes God glorious, like the crown or ornament of a king. 'All the day' is a literal day, from dawn prayer to evening, where we would say 'all day long'.

philological_notes.note: Splendor, beauty, adornment; used of a crown or a glorious garment; here what makes God glorious.

verses.translation_literal: Do not cast me away to a time of old age; when my strength is finished, do not forsake me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not throw me aside when I am old. When my strength runs out, do not leave me.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the turn of the psalm and the reason traditions read it as an old man's prayer: Radak says it was said when David fled Absalom, since he would not have been old when fleeing Saul. Slow down; these are the quietest lines of the chapter.

The verb hišlîk is 'throw away', as one discards a worn tool or sheds a garment, a harsher word than KJV 'cast off'. Old age in the ancient Near East meant loss of status and protection: there was no pension, and an old man's safety rested on children, community and a god. 'Strength' (kōaḥ) is both bodily vigor and ability to win battles. 'Time of old age' (ʿēt ziqnâ) is literally a season, as a time of harvest or war. Malbim and Metzudat David read the fear as how it will look to others: that the victories were only the strength of his own arm.

philological_notes.note: To throw or fling away, as something no longer wanted; stronger than 'cast off'.
'When it comes to an end', from the verb for finishing or being used up.

verses.translation_literal: For my enemies have said [things] to me, and those who watch my life have consulted together,
verses.translation_dramatic: For my enemies have spoken, and those who watch my life have put their heads together,
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason for the plea comes out: a conspiracy. The sentence is left open at the end of the verse and runs on into verse 11, so do not drop the voice. Two groups: the open enemies who speak, and 'those who watch my life', whose watching is ambiguous, either guarding or lying in wait. Radak and Ibn Ezra hear former friends and guards turned traitors; KJV 'lay wait for my soul' picks the hostile meaning.

KJV 'speak against me' and the Hebrew 'to me' differ: the preposition is lî. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it as 'concerning me' (Exodus 14:13), but Malbim takes it literally, that they said it to his face. The word nepeš is here 'life', not 'soul' as KJV has it: they are watching for a chance to take his life. 'They have consulted' (nô'ăṣû) is the council of war, and 'together' (yaḥdāw) stresses the unity of the plot.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who watch my life': guard or ambush. Ibn Ezra and Radak take them as former protectors; Meiri as those who lie in wait for his death.
They have taken counsel together, the formal word for council or conspiracy.

verses.translation_literal: saying: God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is no deliverer.
verses.translation_dramatic: saying, 'God has left him. Run him down. Take him. There is no one to save him.'
verses.directors_commentary:
The conspirators' own words, in direct speech, and the scene turns from the speaker's prayer to the whisper of the pack. The words are short and fast: 'pursue', 'seize'. They have read the speaker's old age and trouble as a sign that God has dropped him, which is the logic of the time: misfortune showed divine abandonment (Rashi: because he already fell into sin; Malbim: because of his sins). That is why verse 9's plea is not self-pity: it concerns God's reputation.

KJV 'persecute' is too weak and too modern; the verb radap is a hunt, to chase on foot. 'Take' (tāp̄aś) is to lay hands on, seize. And 'there is none to deliver' (ʾên maṣṣîl), the participle, takes up the word of verse 2: the enemy says that there is no one who could do what the speaker is asking God to do.

philological_notes.note: Imperative plural, 'chase!': the verb of a hunt or military pursuit.
'One who delivers', from the same root as 'rescue me' (taṣṣîlēnî) in v.2: the enemy claims there is no one to do what the psalmist asks God to do.

verses.translation_literal: God, do not be far from me; my God, to my help make haste.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God, do not stand far off from me. My God, hurry to my help.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer to the whisper: the enemy said 'God has left him', and the speaker says 'do not be far', the direct reply. Ibn Ezra and Radak both note the point: if help is delayed, they will think God is far, so show them otherwise. Two names for God in two lines, 'Elohim' then 'my God', and the second closer and more personal.

The reading in the text is the Ketiv/Qere pair for 'make haste' (ḥûšâ), which does not change the sense. KJV 'make haste for my help' keeps the word order of the Hebrew, which has the help first and the urgent verb last: 'to my help, hurry!' The distance is spatial ('far'), where the enemies talk of abandonment.

philological_notes.note: Imperative 'hurry!'; the packet marks a Ketiv/Qere here, and the sense is unchanged.

verses.translation_literal: May they be ashamed, may they come to an end, the accusers of my self; may they wrap themselves in reproach and ignominy, the seekers of my harm.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be shamed. Let them dwindle and be done, the ones who stand at my side of the court and accuse my very life. Let reproach be pulled about them like a cloak, and disgrace wrapped close, those who go looking for my ruin.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker is an old man, and the voice drops after the plea of v.12. Play this as the other side of the prayer for rescue, not as spite: in a world where there is no police and no appeal, the one who accuses you can ruin you, and shame is the public form of that ruin. The word for accusers, שֹׂטְנֵי, is from the root שׂטן, 'to oppose', the same root that gives the later title 'the Satan', and the KJV's 'adversaries to my soul' keeps the sense but loses the courtroom edge. Then there is the clothing image: יַעֲטוּ is 'wrap themselves', the verb for putting on a mantle, so the shame is worn like a garment (Metzudat David reads it as a covering around the whole body). The KJV's 'confounded and consumed' is a fair sound-match, but 'consumed' is a little too grim for יִכְלוּ, which says only that they come to an end. Note too that נַפְשִׁי is 'my self', or 'my life'; what is at stake is the person, not an abstract soul.

philological_notes.note: Participle 'those who oppose or accuse'. The same root gives the later title 'the Satan'; here it is plain human opposition, perhaps at law. Metzudat Zion ties it to שטן and 'accusation' (קטרוג).
'Wrap themselves', the verb for putting on a cloak. Shame becomes clothing.

token_glosses.gloss: may they come to an end

verses.translation_literal: And I, continually I will wait, and I will add upon all your praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I — I will go on waiting, always waiting; and every praise I have ever given you, I will heap higher still.
verses.directors_commentary:
After four verses of enemies, the speaker puts himself back in the sentence with a hard וַאֲנִי, 'and I', against 'they' in verses 10 to 13. The word is אֲיַחֵל, 'I will wait', and it is waiting with expectation, which is why 'hope' in the KJV is fair. Radak hears it as spoken from inside the trouble: even in distress, I will always wait for you to save me.

The second half is where the KJV paraphrases. It gives "will yet praise thee more and more". The Hebrew says וְהוֹסַפְתִּי עַל־כָּל־תְּהִלָּתֶךָ, 'I will add upon all your praise': it keeps the word 'all' and a counting picture, a total to which more is added. Metzudat David reads it as adding to all that I have praised since then. Radak reads it as adding to what I praised you for in the past troubles once you have saved me; Rashi likewise has the added praise follow the rescue.

Radak also notes that the word is read with the stress on the penult. That stress would mark an ordinary past, 'I have added', as the YLT has it: 'have added unto all Thy praise'. Rashi and Radak, though, still read the sense as future, praise added after the rescue, and so do the two layers here. Malbim goes furthest: every moment new praise accrues, because the speaker survives not by nature but by God's watching, and each moment is a rescue.

philological_notes.note: Pi'el imperfect, 'I will wait, hope'. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'I will hope'. The sense is waiting with expectation, not idle waiting.

From 'to add', in the hiphil, with 'upon': 'I will add upon all your praise'. Radak records a reading with the stress on the penult; that would mark a past 'I have added' (YLT), while Rashi and Radak read the sense as future.

verses.translation_literal: My mouth will recount your righteousness, all the day your salvation, for I have not known numbers.
verses.translation_dramatic: My mouth will tell of your justice. All day long it will tell of your saving. For I never learned the counting of them: there are too many to number.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker boasts of a task he cannot finish. He will 'recount' (יְסַפֵּר) and the word comes from the same root as 'number' (סְפֹרוֹת), so the joke is that a man who tells has no numbers to tell. That wordplay is lost when the KJV writes 'shew forth' in the first half and 'numbers' in the second. Keep it in the voice: 'recount', 'count'. 'All the day' is a literary way of saying 'always', not a clock measure (Radak reads it as 'all the days'). The line is also about a person who does not claim to have a ledger of favours; Metzudat David puts it well: no known number, so he cannot say 'I have finished', and so he goes on telling all day. The word סְפֹרוֹת appears only here, and the commentators (Radak, Meiri) read it as a noun like בְּשׂוֹרוֹת, 'numbers'. 'Righteousness' here is God's justice shown as help, close to 'saving acts', which is why it sits beside 'salvation'.

philological_notes.note: 'He (it) will recount'. The same root gives 'number' (סְפֹרוֹת) at the end of the verse, so telling and counting are one word family.
'Numbers', found only here; Radak and Meiri take it as a noun patterned like בְּשׂוֹרוֹת, Ibn Ezra as patterned like גְּבוּרוֹת.

verses.translation_literal: I will come with the mighty deeds of my Lord YHWH; I will bring to remembrance your righteousness, yours alone.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will come, and I will come carrying the mighty deeds of the Lord GOD. I will call to mind your justice, yours and no one else's.
verses.directors_commentary: 'I will come' needs a place. The Hebrew does not say where, and the commentators split: Radak and Metzudat David hear a man going into battle or into any place at all, trusting God's strength and not the strength of men; Rashi hears a man coming to give thanks. Do not choose for the actors; leave the doorway open. The preposition בְּ in בִּגְבֻרוֹת is 'with' or 'in', and the KJV's 'in the strength of' turns plural 'mighty deeds' into one abstract strength, and drops the sense of a record of deeds he carries with him. 'Lord YHWH' (אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה) is a double title; in the Hebrew reading the second word is spoken as 'Elohim', to avoid saying 'Adonai Adonai'. The last phrase לְבַדֶּךָ, 'yours alone', is polemic: the speaker names no other source of justice, and no other power, human or divine.

philological_notes.note: Plural 'mighty deeds', concrete acts of strength, not the abstract 'strength' of the KJV.
Hiphil 'I will cause to be remembered', that is, 'mention', 'proclaim by name'.

verses.translation_literal: O God, you have taught me from my youth, and until now I declare your wonders.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God, you have been my teacher since I was a boy. And to this very day I am still telling what you have done, the wonders.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the memory of the old man opens: מִנְּעוּרַי, 'from my youth', is the plural word for the years of boyhood and early manhood, and it sets the first part of the arc that closes with 'old age and grey hair' in the next verse. The verb לִמַּדְתַּנִי is 'you taught me', from the root that gives 'disciple' (תַּלְמִיד): the old man is saying that he is God's student. The KJV is accurate here; its only small lapse is 'hitherto', which now sounds antique, where the Hebrew has the plain 'and until now'. אַגִּיד, 'I declare', is a verb of making known publicly, as a herald does; the 'wonders' (נִפְלָאוֹת) are things too marvellous for ordinary explanation. Radak and Metzudat David read the teaching as understanding God gave him to recognise those wonders.

philological_notes.note: 'From my youth'. The plural noun נְעוּרִים names the whole span of early life.
'Your wonders', things set apart as beyond ordinary power.

verses.translation_literal: And also until old age and grey hair, O God, do not forsake me, until I declare your arm to a generation, to every one who will come, your might.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now, even into old age, into white hair, O God, do not leave me. Not until I have told your arm to this generation, and your might to all who are yet to come.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the psalm. The old man does not ask for a long life as such; he asks for enough life to finish telling. The 'until' (עַד) is not a threat to be left afterwards, as Meiri points out: it names the purpose, not the limit. זִקְנָה is old age, and שֵׂיבָה the white hair that is the sign of it; Radak notes that the second is the later stage. The KJV's 'forsake me not' and its 'this generation' are sound, but 'thy strength' for זְרוֹעֲךָ loses the picture: the Hebrew has 'your arm', the body part that throws the spear, the common image of God acting. Notice the cut in the second half: the object 'your might' is held until the very last word, after 'every one who will come', so the future listeners are named before the thing they will hear. In an oral culture, the old are the archive, and Metzudat David says it plainly: fathers tell their sons.

philological_notes.note: 'Your arm', the arm as the organ of force; the usual image for God's saving action. Ibn Ezra glosses 'the strength of your arm'.
'Until I declare'. Meiri argues that עַד here states a purpose and does not imply that God may leave afterwards.

verses.translation_literal: And your righteousness, O God, is up to the height, you who have done great things; O God, who is like you?
verses.translation_dramatic: And your justice, O God, reaches to the heights. You have done great things. O God, who is like you?
verses.directors_commentary: The mood lifts, and the actors' eyes should lift with it. מָרוֹם is the height, a word for the sky and for heaven itself, so God's righteousness is something that has no top. The KJV's 'very high' turns a place into a measure. The verse then runs to the cry 'who is like you?' (מִי כָמוֹךָ), a question that in the ancient Near East had a polemical edge: it was the question asked of other gods, and the answer is understood to be 'no one'. Notice also that 'O God' is said twice, once in the middle, once at the end, so the address is an embrace around the praise. The word גְּדֹלוֹת, 'great things', is the plural of 'great' and means acts of rescue and not size. Rashi joins this verse to the previous one, so that 'your righteousness' is the second thing the speaker will tell the generation to come.

philological_notes.note: 'The height'; the sky and the place of God. The righteousness is not measured as 'high' but reaches there.
A rhetorical question of incomparability; compare the same cry in the song at the sea. The expected answer is 'no one'.

verses.translation_literal: You who have made me see many troubles and calamities, you will return, you will bring me to life; and from the depths of the earth you will return, you will bring me up.
verses.translation_dramatic: You made me look on trouble upon trouble, bitter and many. And you will turn again and give me life. From the deep places of the earth you will turn again, and you will draw me up.
verses.directors_commentary: The text carries a quiet disagreement between writing and reading. The consonants as written say הראיתנו and תחיינו, 'you showed us' and 'you will revive us'; the traditional reading (Qere) says 'me'. Radak, in the packet, takes the plural as the voice of the whole exiled people and the singular as David himself, and he reads this and the rest of the psalm as the exile's voice. We translate the reading, 'me', and keep the other for the reviewer. Notice that God is the one who 'made me see' the troubles: the Hebrew does not hide that in the writer's mind the suffering comes from God, and the KJV's 'shewed' is more careful than the BBE's 'sent'. The twice-repeated תָּשׁוּב, 'you will return', is the heartbeat of the line; the KJV smooths both into 'again'. תְּהֹמוֹת הָאָרֶץ, 'the depths of the earth', is the same word as 'the deep' (תְּהוֹם) in Genesis 1:2, the waters under the world; to be brought up from there is to be brought up from Sheol (Metzudat Zion: 'depth of waters'; Ibn Ezra: the troubles are pictured as being in the depths). The speaker describes near-death as being dead, and the rescue as resurrection from the pit.

philological_notes.note: Ketiv (written) הראיתנו 'you made us see'; Qere (read) הראיתני 'you made me see'. The same pairing at תחיינו / תחייני. Radak understands the written plural as the exile's voice.
'The depths of the earth': the primeval deep under the world, a picture of the grave. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'the depth of waters'.
Repeated before each verb; 'you will turn back, you will revive'. The two-verb pair means 'you will again revive', but the repetition is the rhythm.

token_glosses.gloss: you will bring me to life

verses.translation_literal: May you increase my greatness, and may you turn about, may you comfort me.
verses.translation_dramatic: You will make my greatness grow. You will turn toward me, and you will comfort me.
verses.directors_commentary: A short verse after two long ones; let it be quiet. 'My greatness' (גְּדֻלָּתִי) can mean rank and honour, the opposite of the shame the accusers wished on him; Radak says it will exceed what it was before the exile, and Metzudat David that it is more than rescue. The verb תֶּרֶב is 'you will increase' (a causative, as Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it) and the KJV's 'Thou shalt increase' is fine. The difficulty is וְתִסֹּב. It is the root 'to turn' and 'to go around', and it has no stated object. The KJV's 'on every side' reads it as 'around me' and attaches it to comfort; the ASV's 'turn again' reads it as a turning back; Radak hears God turning his face back to him. The sense is of God coming round, and so the dramatic layer says 'turn toward me', and keeps both readings audible. The pairing recalls the cry in Song of Songs 8:14, 'turn' (סֹב), which Meiri cites.

philological_notes.note: 'My greatness', that is, standing, honour. It echoes גְּדֹלוֹת, the 'great things' God has done, in v.19 (Ibn Ezra).
'And you will turn about'. No object is stated, so it can mean 'turn back to me', 'come around me', or 'go round', and the three give the KJV, ASV and Radak.

verses.translation_literal: Also I, I will praise you with an instrument of lyre, your faithfulness, my God; I will make music to you with a harp, Holy One of Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will thank you, too, with the strings of the lyre, for your faithfulness, my God. I will make music to you on the harp, Holy One of Israel.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the instruments come in, and the scene should have sound. Two are named. The נֶבֶל, a lyre or harp, is the larger, often a jar-shaped or skin-bodied instrument; the כִּנּוֹר is the smaller hand-held lyre, the instrument of David. The KJV 'psaltery' is a medieval European name that no one now knows, and 'harp' for כִּנּוֹר is the right word only if we remember it is a lyre. The phrase בִכְלִי־נֶבֶל is 'with an instrument of lyre', a tool of the lyre kind; the KJV's 'with the psaltery' loses the 'instrument' word, which tells us it is a made object. The attribute אֲמִתְּךָ, 'your faithfulness', is set loose in the clause: it may be the reason for the praise or what is being praised. Radak ties it to the promise that God will keep. The title 'Holy One of Israel' is the great Isaianic title, set at the very end as a signature. Radak adds that in exile he could not play, and now the songs return.

philological_notes.note: A stringed instrument, usually 'lyre' or 'harp'; the KJV 'psaltery' follows the Greek and Latin. The phrase is 'an instrument of lyre'.
'Your faithfulness' or 'your truth'; the stem means what holds firm. Radak ties it to God's promise to bring his people back.
'Holy One of Israel', a title for God. Radak: Israel will hallow his name.

verses.translation_literal: They will ring out, my lips, for I will make music to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed.
verses.translation_dramatic: My lips will ring out, for I will make music to you. And my soul, the soul you bought back, will sing with them.
verses.directors_commentary: Play the verse as a speaker who has run out of one kind of voice and found another. The old man of verse 18 has spoken of gray hair and of enemies; now the weight shifts from speech to song, and from the mouth to the whole person. The plural verb תְּרַנֵּנָּה sits before its subject, 'my lips', so the cry comes first and the mouth after it, as in a shout that is out before the singer has decided to give it. The root רנן is a loud, ringing cry, the sound of a crowd at a victory or a festival, not a murmured hymn. The KJV's 'shall greatly rejoice' turns a sound into a mood and adds the 'greatly' that the Hebrew does not have, and it changes 'for I will sing' into 'when I sing', which makes the joy depend on the singing instead of the other way round. Ibn Ezra reads the doubled nun in this form as a purely grammatical matter: the dagesh makes up for the missing third nun, since the word comes from a geminate root, and he takes the sense to be that when I sing to you, my lips ring out and my soul too. The Hebrew text itself leaves the soul without a verb; the KJV's 'and my soul, which thou hast redeemed' stops in the same place, and the actor should let the line hang for a breath before it ends. The verb פדה is a word from commerce and law: to ransom, to pay the price that frees a person or a firstborn from a claim on them. Here the soul is the object of that payment, and the speaker presents it as already done ('you have redeemed', a completed act), which is why the singing can be certain. Ibn Ezra explains that the soul is named together with the redemption because it rules the body; Radak applies the redemption to the exile, when the heart was not steady and the soul could not take hold of the spirit needed to sing. The BBE's 'in my soul, to which you have given salvation' changes the grammar of the second clause and makes the soul a place instead of a singer. Lips and soul together are the whole voice: the outer mouth that the hearers can hear and the self that is behind it.

philological_notes.note: Third feminine plural imperfect (piel) of רנן, 'to ring out, cry aloud', with the verb before its subject 'my lips'. The doubled nun before the ending is explained by Ibn Ezra as compensation for the missing third nun: the root is geminate, so the form loses one radical and the dagesh stands in for it. The piel is also the usual stem for this verb in psalms of praise, where it names a loud, public cry.

First person cohortative of זמר, 'to make music, to sing with an instrument'. The cohortative ending is a resolve: 'I will make music'. The root is used elsewhere in this psalm for playing the harp and lyre (verse 22), so the singing is joined to instruments, as Rashi and Ibn Ezra say of the lyre.

Second masculine singular perfect of פדה, 'to redeem, to ransom', a word of payment and release. The verb stands with the soul, and Ibn Ezra explains why the soul is named: it rules the body, so what is redeemed with it is the whole person. Radak links it to release from exile.

verses.translation_literal: Also my tongue, all the day, will utter your righteousness; for they are ashamed, for they are abashed, the seekers of my harm.
verses.translation_dramatic: And my tongue, too, will murmur your justice all the day long. For they are shamed. Yes, they are put to shame, those who went seeking my harm.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm closes in a circle. In v.13 the speaker asked for the accusers to be 'ashamed' (יֵבֹשׁוּ) and wrapped in disgrace; here the same root is a fact, בֹּשׁוּ, and the very phrase 'the seekers of my harm' (מְבַקְשֵׁי רָעָתִי) returns word for word. Play the change from wish to report. Two words for shame are given: בֹּשׁוּ and חָפְרוּ; Metzudat Zion says the second too is a word of disgrace. The doubled כִּי, 'for … for …', is a tolling beat, and the KJV's 'confounded … brought unto shame' makes two clauses differ where the Hebrew gives two near-synonyms. The verb תֶּהְגֶּה is 'it will utter' or 'it will murmur', and it is the sound of low, steady speech, as of someone reciting; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'speak'. The tongue is grammatically feminine, so the verb has feminine ending. The statement also finishes the earlier lines about the 'mouth' (v.15) and 'lips' (v.23): the whole body now tells.

philological_notes.note: 'It will utter', a low murmured speech, the sound of recitation or of meditation. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'will speak'.
'They are abashed', a second word for shame beside בֹּשׁוּ; Metzudat Zion calls it a word of disgrace.
